Senses.Explanation: Literally, to let a question descend or to bestow a question. In Chan records it marks a master putting a question to monks and requiring an answer. The heading “questions put in the room” places it in the entering-interview setting; one such question asks how the patriarchal mind-seal is inscribed and how deep the buddhas' source is. A monk later recalls a question bestowed the previous day—“since it is not mind, not buddha, and not a thing, what is it after all?”—and returns to request instruction. Records also show questions put before a group: on a snowy day the master asks why the solitary peak is not white when snow covers the thousand mountains, and elsewhere monks give several replies to “when there is no buddha in the hall, what then?”, none of which the master accepts. The term therefore names an observable part of Chan's interview machinery: the master publicly or privately puts the question, monks answer or fail to answer, and the record preserves the ensuing acceptance, rejection, substitute response, shout, or blow.
Senses.Note: The literal downward/bestowing graph is retained in the alternate target, but ordinary English “put a question” best fits the repeated record headings and speaker turns. It is related to asking (問), public question-and-answer (問答), answers supplied for others (代語), and entering the room (入室), but is not interchangeable with them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中垂問曰：祖師心印，篆作何文？諸佛本源，深之多少？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A room-interview heading introduces two questions put by the master: how the patriarchal mind-seal is written and how deep the buddhas' source is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昨日蒙和尚垂問：既不是心，又不是佛，又不是物，畢竟是甚麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk explicitly recalls having received the master's question the day before and repeats its alternatives.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪日，垂問：「雪覆千山，為什麼孤峰不白？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: On a snowy day the master puts a question and a monk responds in the continuation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師落堂，垂問：「衣裏有珠即不問，堂中無佛時如何？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After entering the hall, the master puts a question; the following monks answer and the master accepts none of their responses.

Senses.Explanation: A lexicalized textual object: the case-preface rubric or a catalogued indication in a recorded-sayings collection. The compound occurs 640 times in 178 allowlisted texts. The fixed rubric “the indication says” (垂示云) occurs 109 times in 21 texts, including 81 in the Blue Cliff Record, where it introduces prefatory pointer prose before the case. One begins, “a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations” (定乾坤句，萬世共遵). Yunmen's Extended Record separately counts “185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers” (室中語要一百八十五則，垂示代語二百九十則). Independent records also carry the section rubric “chamber indication” (室中垂示) before the master's words. A fixed editorial rubric and hundreds of counted textual items establish a textual referent distinguishable from the public act requested of a master.
Senses.Note: This sense is limited to the lexicalized textual rubric/object, not every nominal instance of “indication.” No equation-style self-definition was found, but the fixed rubric and counted collection division independently establish the object. “Indications and substitute answers” (垂示代語) occurs across several texts.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record pointer rubric: ‘the indication says: a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations; a dynamic that captures tigers and rhinoceroses, not distinguished by one thousand sages.’ Editorial case preface, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 垂示云。要道便道。舉世無雙。當行即行。全機不讓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record pointer rubric: ‘the indication says: if you would speak, then speak—unmatched in the world; if you would act, then act—concede nothing of the whole dynamic.’ Editorial preface, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中語要一百八十五則垂示代語二百九十則
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's Extended Record collection heading: ‘185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers.’ A textual division rather than a spoken turn, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中垂示，師云：「五更熟睡時，撞鐘不聞鐘聲，頃寤時鳴鼓，便聞鼓聲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The fixed section rubric “chamber indication” introduces the master's words, independently anchoring the textual-object deployment outside the Blue Cliff Record.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to offer an indication in public exchange
Senses.Explanation: To offer an indication to an addressee in a public exchange. The request “please, master, offer an indication” (請師垂示) occurs 107 times in 56 texts, and “I beg the master to offer an indication” (乞師垂示) occurs 57 times in 26. In one exchange, “within the expedient gate, please, master, offer an indication” is followed by Jiufeng's answer, “buddha does not deprive living beings of their wishes.” In another, Touzi asks Cuiwei and Cuiwei replies, “do you want a second ladle of foul water?” A third request immediately receives “beneath the staff, a shooting star bursts forth” (棒下迸流星). These are requested speaking events, not the separately catalogued case-preface rubric.
Senses.Note: This is not split merely because it is verbal. The public request names an interpersonal speaking event, while the other target explicitly names a fixed editorial rubric or catalogued textual unit; the targets distinguish those referents on their own. Compare question-and-answer (問答), substitute answer (代語), picking up an old case (拈古), verses on old cases (頌古), and raising a case (舉).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：方便門中，請師垂示。師云：佛不奪眾生願。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked to offer an indication, Jiufeng answers that buddha does not deprive living beings of their wishes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子曰。乞師垂示。師曰。更要第二杓惡水那。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Touzi asks Cuiwei to offer an indication; Cuiwei responds with a question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨機一句截断眾流請師垂示師云棒下迸流星
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public interview asks the master to offer an indication and immediately records his reply.

AlternateTargets: like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself” (冷暖自知 / 冷煖自知). Its Zen-specific deployment is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it” (除非親證親悟，方可見得). The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?” (悟道明宗，如人飲水，冷暖自知，云何說其行相), and elsewhere pairs the comparison with “only verification knows; it is difficult to measure” (唯證乃知難可測). Poshan states the same deviation in domestic language: “only each person understands inside his own belly” (只是各人肚裏明白), followed by the water comparison. Thus the corpus retains the ordinary act of drinking but makes the drinker's private knowledge of cold or warmth its recurring Chan predicate.
Senses.Note: The complete stock form has the graphic variants “cold and warm” (冷暖) and “cold and warm” with the alternate graph for warm (冷煖). The short headword is frequently followed immediately by one of them. The Huiming occurrence is a retold early encounter, so it is not linked to a governing speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明上座乃稟言六祖云不思善不思𢙣正當與麼時還我明上座父母未生時面目來明上座於言下忽然默契便禮拜云如人飲水冷暖自知
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings retells the encounter between Huineng and Huiming. Huiming speaks the water comparison after Huineng asks for the face before Huiming's parents were born; this is a raised historical encounter rather than the governing recorder's own speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到這裏如人飲水冷煖自知。除非親證親悟。方可見得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's Recorded Sayings; Dahui directly joins the water comparison to personal verification and understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 悟道明宗。如人飲水。冷暖自知。云何說其行相。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Mirror of the School asks how the manner can be stated when understanding the way is compared to personally knowing water's temperature.

Occurrences.Kwic: 似鏡照容。直須心眼相似。如人飲水。方能冷煖自知。故云唯證乃知難可測。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second, lexicographically distinct deployment in the Record of the Mirror of the School explicitly follows the comparison with “only verification knows.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 只是各人肚裏明白。所謂如人飲水，冷暖自知
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Poshan's Recorded Sayings, under a short address; Poshan supplies the plain predicate “each person understands inside his own belly” before naming the stock comparison.

Senses.Explanation: A stock question in recorded meetings: 'What is Buddha?' (如何是佛). The interrogative asks for the identity or meaning of Buddha, and the record preserves sharply different answers by different masters. Tianyi Yihuai answers, 'spreading the hair to cover mud, laying the body across the ground' (布髮掩泥，橫身臥地); Xuefeng answers, 'Blue sky! Blue sky!' (蒼天，蒼天); Mazu answers, 'this very mind is Buddha' (即心是佛). The translator should preserve the same plain question across these cases so the differing recorded answers remain visible. These are accounts of questions put to named people, not invented literary devices.
Senses.Note: The raw substring occurs 3,795 times in 319 allowlist texts, but that total includes longer expressions such as 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha's teaching?' (如何是佛法大意). Punctuation-specific counts for the standalone question are 446 occurrences of the period form (如何是佛。) in 30 texts and 1,676 occurrences of the question-mark form (如何是佛？) in 237 texts; duplicated recensions and heading material remain included. Use 'What is Buddha?' consistently within a text unless its established English style requires the article.

Occurrences.Kwic: 詰。覺聞，拊几稱善。後七坐道場，化行海內，嗣法者甚眾。住後，僧問：如何是佛？師曰：布髮掩泥，橫身臥地。曰：意旨如何？師曰：任是波旬也皺
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou (越州天衣義懷禪師). The question 'What is Buddha?' receives the answer 'spreading the hair to cover mud, laying the body across the ground.'

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tiansheng Expanded Lamp Record (天聖廣燈錄), Mazu Daoyi. The question 'What is Buddha?' receives Mazu's answer 'this very mind is Buddha' (即心是佛).

Senses.PreferredTarget: what is the central meaning of the buddhas' teaching?
AlternateTargets: what is the main point of the buddhas' teaching?
what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?
Senses.Explanation: A stock public-interview question: literally, 'what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?' In this compound, the law or teaching graph (法) names the teaching under question. The formula occurs 831 times in 125 allowlisted texts and receives no standardized answer. Daolin answers Bai Juyi with 'do no evils; carry out the many goods'; Qingyuan Xingsi asks the price of rice in Luling; Linji shouts, and in another exchange raises the whisk before the monk shouts and Linji strikes; another record answers 'pay your respects,' then cuts off the monk's attempted continuation. A Linji case also records him leaving the Chan seat, seizing Ding, slapping him, and pushing him away. The repeated question is therefore a public demand put to a master, while its recorded answers range across speech, counter-question, shout, implement, and bodily action. The records supply no single answer shared by all these exchanges.
Senses.Note: The phrase itself is one question, not several senses defined by its unlike answers. The ordinary Buddhist-looking wording is bent by the Chan record into an extensively repeated public-interview formula whose answer remains case-specific. Closely related variants such as 'what is the ancestral teacher's meaning in coming from the West?' remain separate questions.

Senses.PreferredTarget: what is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?
AlternateTargets: why did the Patriarch come from the West?
what is the point of the Ancestral Teacher's coming from the West?
what is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?' (如何是祖師西來意: 如何是, 'what is'; 祖師, 'the Patriarch'; 西來, 'coming from the West'; 意, 'meaning or intent'). The Patriarch is Bodhidharma, and the west is India in relation to China. This is the most frequently repeated set question put to masters in the lamp records and recorded sayings: the full eight-graph form occurs 1,858 times in 231 allowlist texts, while the shorter phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意) occurs about 2,081 times. The records preserve different replies by named people. Zhaozhou answers 'the cypress tree in the garden' (庭前柏樹子); Linji, asked while washing his feet, answers 'just now this old monk is washing his feet' (恰值老僧洗脚); National Teacher Huian answers 'why not ask about your own meaning?' (何不問自己意); Mazu says 'lower your voice; come closer' (低聲，近前來) and then strikes the questioner; Jingshan Daoqin says 'your question is improper' (汝問不當); and Damei Fachang answers 'there was no meaning in the coming from the West' (西來無意). The corpus also lists this question and Zhaozhou's answer beside the question 'What is Buddha?' and Dongshan Shouchu's answer 'three catties of hemp' (如何是佛，麻三斤). The entry preserves the plain question so that the different historical answers remain distinct.
Senses.Note: A stock question spoken between two people, not one master's private idiom. MasterName is null on these narrated or raised exchanges; each AttributionNote identifies the questioner and answerer. Compare the shorter noun phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 然則如何是祖師西來意。師云。庭前柏樹子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity (從容庵錄), case 47, 'Zhaozhou's Cypress' (趙州柏樹). A monk first objects, 'do not use an object to show a person' (不將境示人), then asks the question; Zhaozhou answers 'the cypress tree in the garden' (庭前柏樹子). As a raised case, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), section on National Teacher Huian of Mount Song (嵩山慧安國師). Tanran and the young Nanyue Huairang ask the question, and Huian answers, 'Why not ask about your own meaning?' (何不問自己意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州行脚時參師，遇師洗脚次，州便問：如何是祖師西來意？師云：恰值老僧洗脚。

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), section on Damei Fachang of Mingzhou (明州大梅法常). Damei denies the question's premise with 'there was no meaning in the coming from the West' (西來無意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 洪州泐潭法會禪師問馬祖。如何是祖師西來意。祖曰。低聲。近前來。向汝道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元). Fahui of Letan in Hongzhou asks Mazu; Mazu says, 'Lower your voice; come closer; I will tell you' (低聲，近前來，向汝道) and then strikes him.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “what is the way?” Across the Chan record this is a stock public question put to a master. Nanquan answers Zhaozhou, “the ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道); when Zhaozhou asks whether one can head toward it, Nanquan says that intending to head toward it departs from it (擬向即乖). Other records preserve unlike answers without a single harmonizing gloss: “white clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies love the courtyard flowers” (白雲覆青嶂，蜂蝶戀庭華), “every household's gate opens onto Chang'an” (家家門口通長安), and “what is sweet is licorice” (甜底是甘草). One master merely rebuffs the question and sends the monk away. In a longer written questionnaire, the answer begins “unobstructed is the Way” (無礙是道). Zhaozhou's record also makes the ordinary road-word audible: the master first answers “the one outside the wall” (墻外底); when the monk says he means the great Way, the answer is “the great road runs through Chang'an” (大道透長安). The dictionary therefore retains the literal question and its observable public-interview role; the mutually different recorded answers are not converted into an interpretive menu.
Senses.Note: Capitalize “Way” when the exchange distinguishes it from an ordinary road, but translate the road wordplay explicitly where it occurs.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道。州云。還可趣向否。泉云。擬向即乖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Nanquan–Zhaozhou public case and its immediate follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師曰。白雲覆青嶂。蜂蝶戀庭華。

Occurrences.Kwic: 一問。如何是道。何以修之。為復必須修成。為復不假功用。答。無礙是道。覺妄是修。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A written ten-question sequence supplies a direct answer formula rather than a short encounter reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師便咄。僧曰。學人未領旨。師曰。去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question receives a rebuff; the monk's request for clarification is answered with “go.”
